content: Over the years, WASH accounts have proven to be a critical tool in raising awareness among decision-makers about funding gaps in the water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) sector. These accounts have also supported progressive increases in sector funding by influencing discussions on funding allocations across the sector. For example, in Mali, improved knowledge of sector financing has led to increased funding allocations, as documented in various reports and personal communications. In Ghana, the Asutifi North District Assembly initiated a comprehensive WASH master plan in 2018 to address the challenges of reaching underserved populations and improving service levels in rural areas and small towns. This plan included a clear vision, mediumand long-term strategies, a costed plan with identified funding sources, and a monitoring and evaluation framework. Since 2018, annual data collection has been conducted to monitor the implementation of the master plan, using indicators aligned with national frameworks. This has strengthened evidence-based decision-making and resource allocation, leading to actions such as doubling the district WASH budget from 2018 to 2019 and improving coordination among partners. In Nepal, the development of the National Water Supply, Sanitation, and Hygiene Management Information System in 2018 addressed the lack of a consolidated data management system. This system integrates data from urban and rural contexts, covering sustainability, functionality, and water quality indicators. It has enabled stakeholders, including government ministries and development partners, to use georeferenced data for planning and decision-making, such as the development of national and subnational plans. In Latin America and Africa, the Rural Water and Sanitation Information System (SIASAR), launched in 2011, has expanded to cover 15 countries and over 5 million rural inhabitants. This system provides a unified platform for monitoring, planning, and evaluating rural water and sanitation services. It harmonizes tools and approaches, allowing for comparative data analysis across sites and countries. In Colombia, for instance, SIASAR has supported planning and funding decisions for water access in Indigenous and rural communities, as well as prioritizing water supply construction in underserved municipalities. In Ethiopia, a 2022 water quality assessment in three districts involved testing water samples from community water points, schools, healthcare facilities, and households. The findings, presented in simplified and visual formats, were shared with local government actors and community members to prioritize resources and take corrective actions. This approach motivated community-led initiatives, such as fencing water points and requesting water chlorination. In Kenya and Tanzania, regulators produce annual performance reports benchmarking water service providers against key indicators. These reports, presented in visual formats with traffic-light color coding, highlight changes over time and are aligned with annual planning and budgeting cycles. They also include follow-ups with water suppliers to ensure corrective measures are implemented. In Vanuatu, the government systematically uses data on water safety risks to inform routine funding allocations. This approach aligns with the National Sustainable Development Plan 2016–2030, which emphasizes evidence-based decision-making to achieve sustainable development goals.
